newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity ends up on SW heat, firmer cash.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity ends up on SW heat, firmer cash.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures settled sharply higher Monday on return of hot, dry weather in the Southwest and firmer spot physical prices across the West.
Asked about the factor behind today's rally, one Northwest futures trader said, "People are looking at these 105, 110 (degrees F) readings (in the Southwest interior section)."

Meanwhile, temperatures in the Pacific Northwest were expected to be one to five degrees below normal early in the week, then were forecast to be near normal for the middle of the week and cool again to just below normal late in the week. Clouds and showers were expected early in the week.

Firm, peak power prices for Tuesday at the Palo Verde (PV) switchyard in Arizona rose two dollars to $19.50-20.50, while those at the California Oregon Border (COB) were steady at $14.00-15.00 despite more than 2,000 megawatts (MW) of coal-fired generation restored to operation over the weekend.
"People were expecting more generation to come back," said a West Coast electricity broker.
Weekend restart of a 300 MW Reid Gardner coal-fired unit was pushed back to Thursday and startup of a 260 MW Hayden coal-fired unit was postponed to early July.

Nevertheless, another 1,000 MW of coal-fired capacity is scheduled to return online Tuesday. and the 1,112 MW WNP-2 nuclear power plant in Washington state was expected to resume power production later this week.
July PV futures settled up $1.61 a megawatt hour (MWh) at $29.29 after posting a session high at $29.50. It partially filled a price gap at $29.50-30.30.
August PV finished up $1.12 at $30.98. Other PV contracts ended 45 to 79 cents higher.
July COB settled up $1.53 a MWh at $19.33, near its session high of $19.50 and partially filled a price gap at $19.25-20.25.
August COB finished up $1.49 at $22.40. Deferred COB months ended 70 to 86 cents higher.

Some upward pressure on futures was came from expecations a Western Systems Coordinating Council committee this week would propose a summertime rating for the Pacific Intertie at 6,900 megawatt (MW) from the current limit of 7,200 MW.
In the meantime, Bonneville Power Administration suggested summer transmission capacity on the intertie be reduced to 6,300, down 900 MW from current level.
NYMEX estimated 935 COB and 922 PV contracts were sold.
